content: 1. Famciclovir administered for 5 days and 10 days was evaluated in three randomized trials to assess the duration of lesions from the onset of treatment, measured by the median time to complete healing. The trials demonstrated a median healing time of 7–8 days for both durations, indicating similar outcomes. The quality of evidence was moderate, and the outcome was deemed important. 2. Pain and quality of life were not measured in these studies. Adverse events, specifically drug toxicity, were assessed in three randomized trials. Mild nausea and dizziness were reported as adverse events associated with famciclovir. The quality of evidence was moderate, and the outcome was considered critical. 3. The duration of symptoms from the onset of treatment, measured by the time to loss of symptoms, was evaluated in three randomized trials. The median duration was 6–8 days for the 5-day treatment and 8–12 days for the 10-day treatment, with similar outcomes observed. The quality of evidence was moderate, and the outcome was considered important. 4. HSV-2 transmission and compliance were not measured in these studies. The duration of viral shedding, measured by the median time to cessation of viral shedding, was assessed in three randomized trials. The median duration was 2–3 days for both treatment durations, with similar outcomes. The quality of evidence was moderate, and the outcome was considered important. 5. High-dose acyclovir (4 g daily for 10 days) was compared to standard-dose acyclovir (1 g daily for 10 days) in a randomized trial. The time to first recurrence was reduced by a median of 8 days (range: 11–196 days fewer) with high-dose acyclovir. However, the quality of evidence was very low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. The outcome was considered important. 6. The duration of viral shedding was also compared between high-dose and standard-dose acyclovir in a randomized trial. Both doses resulted in a median duration of 3 days. The quality of evidence was low, and the outcome was considered important. 7. The WHO guidelines for the treatment of genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) recommend episodic therapy for recurrent episodes. The main outcomes of interest include HSV-2 transmission, HSV-2 shedding, severity of symptoms, quality of life, side effects, compliance, ulcer healing, and duration of clinical episodes. Oral antiviral medications such as acyclovir, famciclovir, and valaciclovir are used for initial, episodic, and suppressive therapy, but there is no cure for the infection. 8. In 2012, it was estimated that over 417 million people globally were infected with HSV-2, with higher prevalence in lowand middle-income countries. Recurrent episodes occur in 20–50% of individuals, with a median recurrence rate of four episodes in the first year. Recurrence rates typically decrease over time but increase in about one-quarter of patients. Immunosuppressed individuals experience more severe and frequent recurrences. HSV-2 infection also increases the risk of acquiring HIV and can be transmitted to neonates from infected pregnant mothers. 9. Thirteen reports of 16 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in a systematic review comparing treatment with no treatment and different drugs/dosages. Acyclovir, valaciclovir, and famciclovir were evaluated. Valaciclovir likely reduces the duration of viral shedding by a median of 2 days and lesions/symptoms by 1–2 days compared to placebo. Famciclovir likely reduces the duration of viral shedding, lesions, and symptoms by a median of 1–2 days compared to placebo. The benefits were small, and the harms were trivial across drugs and no treatment. 10. Comparisons between acyclovir, valaciclovir, and famciclovir showed little-to-no differences in outcomes such as duration of viral shedding, lesions, symptoms, and adverse events. The quality of evidence ranged from low to moderate. Different dosages of acyclovir, valaciclovir, and famciclovir were also compared, with little-to-no differences observed in outcomes. 11. The cost of treatment per episode was moderate for acyclovir but increased with recurrence. Costs were higher for valaciclovir and famciclovir. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) agreed that cost-effectiveness did not favor any specific drug, as the benefits were small and the costs moderate. 12. The GDG discussed the potential impact on health equity. While there was probably no impact on equity overall, the use of more costly drugs like valaciclovir and famciclovir could reduce equity. The GDG concluded that there was little variability in the balance of effects between interventions and comparisons. 13. Patient preferences for genital herpes treatment were influenced by factors such as recurrence risk reduction, number of tablets taken daily, and cost. Stigma related to the condition was also an important consideration. The GDG agreed that the intervention was probably acceptable to key stakeholders.
